To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the methylation of nuclear DNA in plants increases with increasing DNA GC-content and that this methylation gradient is different in different species, and therefore represents a new, characteristic genome feature.

(a) the GC-rich, noncoding sequences of plant nuclear DNA are methylated in a GC-rich, nonrandom pattern; (b) this methylation is a novel, characteristic plant genome feature; (c) the methylation pattern is not related to the methylation status of the transposable elements; and (d) it may represent an important structural feature of plant genomes.

the methylation of plant genomes is not uniform, and that the noncoding sequences, which make up the bulk (about 90%) of the plant genome, show a characteristic methylation gradient from GC-poor (hypomethylated) to GC-rich (hypermethylated) sequences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the methylation patterns in plant genomes.
the study of DNA methylation patterns in nuclear genomes of plants and animals.
the structural features of the plant nuclear genome and with the functional implications of these features.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the methylation pattern is not random, but that it follows a certain order.

the methylation gradient is a characteristic feature of plant nuclear DNA and is probably a consequence of the presence of a high proportion of repetitive sequences in the intergenic fraction of plant nuclear genomes.
methylation is not randomly distributed in the genome of the plants investigated but is rather concentrated in the GC-rich, repetitive, intergenic DNA sequences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the methylation patterns of nuclear DNA in the plant species investigated are highly complex and show a large degree of variability.
the methylation patterns in plants are not random but are highly ordered, which suggests that the methylation of plant nuclear DNA is under some sort of control.
methylation is a widespread and important phenomenon in plants, but that it is not a random process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the methylation of plant genomes is a complex process which is not limited to a few genes and gene regulatory sequences, and that the methylation patterns of plant genomes are not uniform.
methylation of DNA is not a random process, but is highly organized in plants, and that the methylation gradient may reflect the functional importance of DNA methylation.
the plant genome contains large amounts of repetitive sequences that are methylated and, thus, silenced.
